title: Regional denial + GPU pool scarcity experiment: controlled degradation and dependency-blackhole validation
creator: Aisha Romero
description: Summary: Run a controlled, repeatable experiment that simulates a single-region control-plane denial combined with progressive GPU pool scarcity and upstream dependency blackholes. The goal is to validate graceful degradation strategies (routing fallbacks, admission control, circuit breakers, load-shedding thresholds) and verify SLO behavior and alerting during compound failures. This ticket defines the experiment matrix, safety guardrails, observable signals, and acceptance criteria for the run. Background: Recent on-call incidents and tabletop reviews highlighted cases where a region lost partial control-plane connectivity while downstream storage and auth dependencies experienced elevated latencies. We need a deterministic harness to exercise the combined failure modes and confirm that client-facing SLOs degrade predictably and the console/ops playbook surfaces the right mitigations.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Reproducible test harness that can induce: (a) control-plane region denial (control plane API returns 5xx / timeouts); (b) GPU pool starvation (simulated by limiting available pods and introducing backpressure); and (c) dependency blackholes (targeted TCP drops to select internal services).
2) When under test, critical SLOs (p95 < target for low-tier region traffic) either remain within degraded SLA documented in runbook OR automatic fallback to secondary region/model variant occurs within configured window.
3) Circuit breakers and admission controls trigger at configured thresholds and prevent system-wide meltdown in >95% of trials.
4) All monitoring dashboards, dashboards, and synthetic checks capture the experiment signals and generate the expected alert noise profile.
5) No customer data is exfiltrated and audit log entries exist for every injected action.
test_plan:
Phases:
- Phase 0 (dry run): deploy canary harness to staging with safety toggles (kill-switch + scoped CIDR). Verify observability.
- Phase 1 (region denial only): simulate control-plane API timeouts for region 'us-west-2' for 10m windows and observe routing/fallback.
- Phase 2 (gpu pressure): gradually reduce available GPU worker replicas (50% -> 20% -> 0) while generating realistic inference traffic profiles with token distribution and kv-cache hit rates. Measure queueing, latencies, internal rate limits.
- Phase 3 (compound): run region denial concurrently with GPU scarcity and introduce dependency blackholes against auth-service and model-store for 5m windows.
- Phase 4 (blameless postmortem): collect traces, logs, dashboards, and runbook timelines.
Injection methods:
- Control-plane denial via feature-flagged proxy that returns 504 for control-plane endpoints.
- GPU scarcity via scheduler shim that marks GPUs as unschedulable and scaling policies tied to test harness.
- Dependency blackhole via iptables rules on a subset of dependency hosts in the test VPC.
Safety guardrails: scoped to non-production account, kill-switch triggers that restore all routes on two consecutive operator confirmations, automated rate limits on traffic generator, and preflight checks for customer traffic isolation.
monitoring_and_alerting: Dashboards to validate: per-region p50/p95/p99 latencies, admission-control rejects per-second, queue depth, model variant fallback count, token cost delta, and error budget burn. Alerts: SLO burn >20% in 10m, fallback rate >10% for 5m, circuit-breaker open count >3 across services. Also attach a 'noise' suppression rule during the experiment window to avoid paging on known test alerts but still record them in the incident timeline.
rollback_playbook:
1) Hit kill-switch -> disable all fault-injection proxies.
2) Scale GPU worker pools back to baseline via autoscaler override.
3) Restore iptables rules.
4) If automated rollback does not converge in 3 minutes, invoke manual region failover steps described in runbook.
5) Post-rollback, run full health check and synthetic end-to-end tests before marking system 'green'.
